name: theworldofai.org AI Laws: state AI bill tracker and patterns
title: theworldofai.org AI Laws: state AI bill tracker and patterns
answer: Theworldofai.org's AI Laws section is a live tracker of US state artificial intelligence legislation. It says it follows 6,015 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions, updated daily from LegiScan, and it summarises 103 passed measures across 27 states reviewed on September 18, 2026. Its most useful point is that no two states wrote the same law, yet the same duties recur: AI may assist but not be the only decider in high stakes decisions, and attorneys general are the enforcers most likely to act.

sections.body: It is published on theworldofai.org as the site's AI Laws section. The text describes a live tracker of United States state artificial intelligence legislation, covering 6,015 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions and refreshed daily from the LegiScan legislative database, with links to each bill's official page. It also says the site built pages from the enrolled text of 103 AI measures across 27 states and reviewed them on September 18, 2026. The page sits within a wider atlas that includes a lawsuit tracker, glossary, tools directory, AI companies, research library, MCP server registry, compliance frameworks, sources, people, calculators and weekly digests. It says every page is rebuilt daily from primary sources, carries the date it was last verified, and is free to read, free to cite and free to query. The same text promotes books by Stephen R. Jordan and SRJ Consulting & Services, including The AI Lawyer, a novel out on 17 August 2026.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The source says United States AI legislation is written state by state, and it tracks all of it. It reports 6,015 artificial intelligence bills across 53 jurisdictions, refreshed daily from LegiScan and linked to each bill's official page. It then describes a comparison of 103 measures across 27 states that a state has passed, reviewed on September 18, 2026. The source says no two states wrote the same law, but the same choices keep appearing. Only two states passed a broad law that reaches consequential decisions across sectors, Colorado in CO SB189 and Texas in TX HB149. Every other measure names one setting, such as a companion chatbot, a political ad, an insurance prior authorization, a classroom or a state agency. Where the stakes are personal, legislatures keep writing the same rule: AI may assist, but it may not be the only decider. Insurers cannot deny care on an algorithm alone. New York requires meaningful human review before agencies automate benefit decisions. No state in this set created a new agency to enforce AI law. The attorney general enforces the larger laws. The source advises building to the common core: tell people when they are dealing with AI, keep a qualified person in any decision about health, employment, benefits or education, have a crisis protocol and know the age of your user if your product holds a conversation, and keep records of what the system does, because the attorney general is the enforcer you are most likely to meet.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source gives these figures and positions. It says it tracks 6,015 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions, updated daily from LegiScan. It says it compared 103 measures across 27 states, reviewed on September 18, 2026. It says only two states passed a broad law reaching consequential decisions across sectors, Colorado in CO SB189 and Texas in TX HB149. It says no state in this set created a new agency to enforce AI law. It says the attorney general enforces the larger laws, often exclusively, citing CA SB53, CO SB189, GA SB540, ID S1297, IL SB0315, NY S06953, RI H7350 and TX HB149. It says several states declare a violation to be an unfair or deceptive trade practice under their consumer protection act, citing CT HB05222, HI SB3001, ME LD1727, TN HB1470 and WA HB2225. It says a private right to sue is the exception, appearing mainly where one identifiable person is harmed. It says insurers cannot deny care on an algorithm alone, citing AL SB63 and IA HF2635. It says AI cannot deliver therapy or present itself as a licensed clinician, citing IL HB1806, TN HB1470 and CA AB489. It says AI cannot be the sole instructor of a college course or score a teacher evaluation, citing IL HB1859 and IL SB2909. It says New York requires meaningful human review before agencies automate benefit decisions, citing NY S07599. It says the site is free to read, free to cite and free to query, and every page is rebuilt daily from primary sources and carries the date it was last verified. It also says The AI Lawyer, a novel by SRJ Consulting & Services, is out on 17 August 2026.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: A reader following AI in Government can use this source to see the state by state patchwork that agencies and contractors face. It directly notes New York's requirement for meaningful human review before agencies automate benefit decisions, and it says no state created a new agency to enforce AI law, leaving attorneys general as the main enforcers. That matters for government AI oversight, because the source says the attorney general enforces the larger laws, often exclusively, and several states treat violations as unfair or deceptive trade practices. It also helps a government reader track which settings legislatures name, such as state agencies, classrooms, insurance prior authorization and political ads. The source is a tracker and summary, not legal advice, but it links to official bill pages and says it is free to cite and query.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Government

sections.body: The source text is a landing page and tracker summary, not a full legal analysis. It focuses on US state AI bills and does not mention federal legislation or a federal register watch. It gives 6,015 bills, and it does not explain how that figure relates to the 103 passed measures it compares. It summarises 103 measures across 27 states, so it is partial relative to the 6,015 bills it says it tracks. It is commercial: it promotes books by Stephen R. Jordan, SRJ Consulting & Services, audits and a novel. It is dated by its review on September 18, 2026, and its daily LegiScan refresh, while the supplied text was harvested on September 29, 2026. It does not cover enforcement outcomes, court decisions or practical compliance steps beyond the common core it lists.
